title: The Tide of the Crescent Cove
premise: Silas Ishikawa has spent eleven years raising his daughter alone in Crescent Cove, telling himself the heart can be trained into stillness after the woman he loved vanished without a word. When a storm-damaged mail sack yields a letter she wrote the week she disappeared — a letter that reveals she left to protect him from her family's criminal debts, not because she stopped loving him — Silas must confront his own cowardice in never searching for her. As he follows the letter's clues, he discovers she returned to the cove two years ago and has been living quietly nearby, too ashamed to face him. The story ends with Silas choosing forgiveness over pride: he forgives himself first for the years of silence, then finds her at the tide line where they first met, and they begin again slowly, honestly, with his daughter's blessing.
about_author: Gideon Reyes is a former coastal bookseller who writes love stories about second chances and small towns that keep secrets. He lives on the Pacific Northwest shore with his partner and an aging dog named Marginalia.

chapters.title: The Weight of Ordinary Days
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. We meet Silas running Tidewater Books, raising fourteen-year-old Hana, and performing contentment so well he almost believes it. A routine morning establishes his routines-as-armor. Emotional beat: quiet loneliness disguised as discipline.

chapters.title: What the Storm Gave Back
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. After a winter storm, harbor workers recover an old mail sack; inside is a water-stained letter addressed to Silas, postmarked eleven years ago. He recognizes the handwriting instantly and cannot bring himself to open it. Emotional beat: dread tangled with desperate hope.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Silas finally reads the letter: Mari left because her father's debts endangered Silas and baby Hana, and she believed disappearing was love. Flashbacks reveal their romance. Emotional beat: grief reframed — betrayal becomes sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Clue in the Postmark
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. The postmark shows the letter was mailed from a town two hours north, meaning Mari was close, alive, and chose silence. Silas begins investigating against Hana's warnings. Emotional beat: obsession kindling beneath rational caution.

chapters.title: Hana's Map
chapters.summary: Hana's POV. Hana, furious and frightened, admits she once found a birthday card from 'M' and hid it. She gives Silas a return address she memorized years ago. Emotional beat: a daughter's protective anger softening into complicity.

chapters.title: The Woman at the Harbor Light
chapters.summary: Mari's POV. We see Mari's eleven years: hiding, working a cannery, learning Silas remarried nothing and no one — but believing Hana deserved better than a fugitive mother. She has watched the bookshop from afar. Emotional beat: shame as self-imposed exile.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas travels north, finds Mari's cottage empty — she fled hours before, tipped off by a neighbor. He realizes she is running again, and this time he refuses to let her. Emotional beat: frustration hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Debts Unpaid
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Silas uncovers the truth about her father's creditors — most dead or imprisoned, the threat long expired — but also learns Mari paid anonymous restitution for years. Justice outside the law, done in secret. Emotional beat: admiration replacing resentment.

chapters.title: The Tide Line
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POV. During the spring festival, Silas guesses where she'll be: the cove's tide line where they first met. Confrontation in the rain — accusations, confessions, and Silas's admission that his own silence and pride built the prison they both lived in. Emotional beat: catharsis.

chapters.title: A Heart, Retrained
chapters.summary: Resolution, Silas's POV. Months later: Mari works the shop's back counter, Hana sets a third plate without ceremony, and forgiveness proves less a moment than a practice. Silas concedes the heart isn't containable after all — it's trainable toward openness. Emotional beat: earned, unshowy belonging.
